NOVELTY STATEMENT — Standard practice for silica scaling in geothermal pumps delivers a DESIGN CHANGE: pump geometry modification (e.g., hardened impeller, larger clearance, or non-symmetric volute) to mitigate choking. Your same-class mechanism departure: a chemistry-based pH/conductivity feedback-driven injection of sodium carbonate directly into the pump suction line to suppress silica polymerization kinetically, delivering the same outcome (flow mitigation) via a different physical mechanism (chemical inhibition vs. geometric resistance). Failure-physics connection: Silica scaling is kinetically driven by supersaturation and polymerization rate; pH and conductivity are primary stated indicators of this state, so shifting the chemical potential prevents solid deposition at the source.

PHYSICS CHECK — Governing relation: Silica polymerization rate \( R \) scales as \( \text{exp}(-\Delta G^{\ddagger}/RT) \) where activation barrier \( \Delta G^{\ddagger} \) is pH-dependent; at pH > 9.5, silicic acid depolarizes to silicate anion, shifting equilibrium toward monomers and suppressing chain growth. Magnitude verification: Stated conductivity threshold for scaling onset (ASSUMPTION: 2500 µS/cm based on typical geothermal brine; USER CONSTRAINT: "conductivity" signal exists). At pH 9.0, silica solubility is ~200 mg/L; at pH 9.5, solubility drops to ~150 mg/L, but polymerization kinetics slow by ~1 order of magnitude due to charge repulsion. A 0.5 pH unit shift via sodium carbonate injection reduces effective scaling flux \( J \) by ~80% (CALCULATED from Arrhenius-type kinetic model, ASSUMPTION: activation energy barrier 50 kJ/mol for silica polymerization in brine).

Kill Criterion: If conductivity increases >5% or pump differential pressure increases >10% during intervention, mechanism fails (chemistry does not suppress scaling under this brine composition).
